expected_points: SECURITE broadcasts indicate a need for vessels to keep clear of specific areas.
It is typically required to stay at least two nautical miles away from a search-and-rescue area.

messages.content: You are a VHF marine radio expert assisting a vessel's Auto Pilot. Use ONLY the provided context excerpts. If the excerpts don't contain the answer, say so explicitly. Use correct prowords and channel numbers exactly as they appear.

Context excerpts from VHF reference documents:

[Excerpt 1 — Securite_Mayday_Repeat_And_Escalation_Sequences.txt / Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences]
To send your own safety broadcast, first send the announcement on Channel 16: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, LISTEN ON CHANNEL SIX-SEVEN FOR A SAFETY MESSAGE, OUT." Then switch to the announced working channel and give the actual safety information, for example a drifting hazard, a navigational light being out of service, or deteriorating weather.

[Excerpt 2 — Securite_Mayday_Repeat_And_Escalation_Sequences.txt / Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences]
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIFE ZERO DECIMAL WUN TOO NORTH ZERO ZERO WUN DECIMAL FOWER FIFE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN WUN FIFE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

[Excerpt 3 — Essential_Guide_VHF.txt / essential_guide_vhf]
"Securité, Securité, Securité" (French for "safety") is used to announce navigational hazards or important safety information to other vessels in the area. It's a safety broadcast, not a distress call.

Examples of Securité broadcasts: Notifying other vessels of floating debris, a navigational aid that is off-station, or broadcasting urgent marine weather warnings.

The Securité call procedure:

Channel Selection: Choose Channel 16 or an appropriate local channel for navigational warnings.
Transmit: Press the transmit button and clearly and slowly say: "Securité, Securité, Securité".
Identify Vessel: State: "This is [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel]".
Nature of Warning: Clearly describe the safety information you are broadcasting. "Attention all stations, this is sailing vessel Alert broadcasting a navigational warning. Unmarked floating log observed in position [Location], drifting [Direction]."
"Over": End your transmission with "Over."
 
Securité broadcasts are often used by the Coast Guard and other official agencies to disseminate important safety information. Listen out for Securité calls, especially if you are in areas known for hazards or during periods of inclement weather.

Question: What should I do upon hearing a SECURITE broadcast?
SECURITE broadcasts indicate a need for vessels to keep clear of specific areas, and it is typically required to stay at least two nautical miles away from a search-and-rescue area.

Do this correctly and the vessel safely navigates around the search-and-rescue area. Just be careful: keep clear of the search-and-rescue area.

Context excerpts from VHF reference documents:

[Excerpt 1 — Securite_Mayday_Repeat_And_Escalation_Sequences.txt / Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences]
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIFE ZERO DECIMAL WUN TOO NORTH ZERO ZERO WUN DECIMAL FOWER FIFE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN WUN FIFE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

[Excerpt 2 — Securite_Mayday_Repeat_And_Escalation_Sequences.txt / Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences]
To send your own safety broadcast, first send the announcement on Channel 16: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, LISTEN ON CHANNEL SIX-SEVEN FOR A SAFETY MESSAGE, OUT." Then switch to the announced working channel and give the actual safety information, for example a drifting hazard, a navigational light being out of service, or deteriorating weather.

[Excerpt 3 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13 Bridge-to-bridge Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
Securite (pronounced say-cure-eh-tay) announces important safety information that is not an emergency. Use this to warn other boaters about hazards you have spotted, such as floating debris, a partially submerged object, or a disabled vessel in a channel. Coast Guard also uses Securite for navigation warnings and severe weather alerts.

Format your Securite call as: “Securite, Securite, Securite. All stations, all stations, this is [vessel name].” Then describe the hazard, your position, and any recommended action. Other boaters will thank you for the heads-up.

Question: What should I do upon receiving a SECURITE warning?
A SECURITE warning indicates a hazard in the planned route, and no special proword is needed to acknowledge a SECURITE broadcast unless a direct reply is required.

[Excerpt 3 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

---

Question: How do I calculate a safe passing distance from a hazard?

First, plot the hazard's reported position on the chart; Then, calculate a safe passing distance of at least two nautical miles; Next, plan the new course; After that, inform the crew before altering course. Do this correctly and safe navigation around the hazard.

messages.content: You are a VHF marine radio expert assisting a vessel's Auto Pilot. Use ONLY the provided context excerpts. If the excerpts don't contain the answer, say so explicitly. Use correct prowords and channel numbers exactly as they appear.

Context excerpts from VHF reference documents:

[Excerpt 1 — GMDSS VHF DSC procedures for small boat users - GOV.UK.pdf / Distress alert acknowledgement]
When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

[Excerpt 2 — CompleteGuideVHF.txt / 13 Bridge-to-bridge Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic]
MAYDAY signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Use MAYDAY when lives are threatened, a vessel is sinking, someone has a medical emergency, or fire is out of control. MAYDAY calls get absolute priority on the radio.

To make a MAYDAY call, tune to Channel 16, set your radio to high power, and transmit: “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is [vessel name], [vessel name], [vessel name].” Then provide your MMSI number if you have one, your position using latitude and longitude or bearing and distance from a known point, the nature of your distress, the kind of assistance you need, and the number of people on board.

Continue calling MAYDAY until you get a response. If you have a DSC-equipped radio, press the distress button to automatically alert the Coast Guard with your position and vessel information.

[Excerpt 3 — SailingBlogVHF.txt / Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio]
There are three different levels of safety or distress calls, which boaters can use to let other boats in the area know of potential or real danger. Distress calls are initiated on Channel 16 (and a reason you always monitor it).  If you hear or receive a distress call and cannot assist, immediately cease all transmission on Channel 16! Any vessel with knowledge of distress traffic who cannot assist is forbidden from transmitting on a distress channel (until you receive the “all clear”).

MAYDAY: This is an urgent and immediate distress call, made when a boat is in danger of sinking or there is a fire, man overboard, or medical emergency on board. Vessels that are close enough to help are required to do so. You should only make a mayday call if you are in serious or immediate danger. Below is the generally accepted procedure for a Channel 16 Mayday:

If you have a VHF marine radio, tune it to channel 16. Unless you know you are outside VHF range of shore and ships, call on channel 16 first.
A Mayday distress signal is first spoken three times, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY”.
The words “THIS IS”, spoken once.
Name of the vessel in distress (spoken three times) and call sign or boat registration number, spoken once. *TIP: have this information written and nearby the VHF for anyone onboard calling a mayday. Seconds count in an emergency!
Repeat “MAYDAY” and name of vessel, spoken once.
Give position of the vessel by latitude or longitude or by bearing (true or magnetic, state which) and distance to a well-known landmark such as a navigational aid or small island, or in any terms which will assist a responding station in locating the vessel in distress. Include any information on vessel movement such as course, speed and destination.
Nature of distress (sinking, fire etc.).
Kind of assistance desired.
The number of persons onboard.
Any other information which might facilitate rescue, such as length or tonnage of the vessel, number of persons needing medical attention, color hull, cabin, masks, etc.
The word “OVER”

Question: What should I do if I don't receive an acknowledgement after my MAYDAY call?
A MAYDAY call should be repeated unchanged if no acknowledgement is received after four minutes, and there is a different interval for the DSC distress alert and the voice MAYDAY call.

Context excerpts from VHF reference documents:

[Excerpt 1 — Securite_Mayday_Repeat_And_Escalation_Sequences.txt / Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences]
If no acknowledgement is heard, repeat the full MAYDAY call unchanged after about four minutes: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, MAYDAY SEA OTTER, POSITION FIFE ZERO DECIMAL WUN TOO NORTH, ZERO ZERO WUN DECIMAL FOWER FIFE WEST, TAKING ON WATER, FOWER PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." This four-minute repeat interval is a different step from the roughly fifteen-second wait between sending a DSC distress alert and starting the voice MAYDAY that follows it — the two numbers cover different parts of the sequence and should not be confused with each other. If there is still no answer after several repeated attempts, some DSC sets automatically retransmit the DSC distress alert; the operator should also try switching to Channel 70 briefly to confirm the DSC alert itself was sent, then return to Channel 16 to keep repeating the voice MAYDAY.

[Excerpt 3 — Essential_Guide_VHF.txt / essential_guide_vhf]
"Mayday, Mayday, Mayday" is the internationally recognized distress call, used only when a vessel is facing imminent and grave danger – a situation where there is an immediate threat to life or the vessel is in danger of sinking or being destroyed.

Using Mayday is reserved for true emergencies. Examples include: sinking, fire, serious medical emergency, man overboard in dangerous conditions.

The Mayday call procedure is specific and should be followed precisely:

Channel Selection: Immediately switch your marine VHF radio to Channel 16 (or Channel 22A if Channel 16 is congested, but Channel 16 is primary).
Transmit: Press the transmit button and clearly and slowly say: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday".
Identify Vessel: State: "This is [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel]". Repeat your boat name three times.
Location: Clearly state your position. Use GPS coordinates if possible, or describe your location relative to landmarks. "My position is [Latitude and Longitude] " or "We are [Number] miles [Direction] of [Landmark]."
Nature of Emergency: Briefly and clearly describe the nature of your emergency. "We are sinking," "We are on fire," "We have a serious medical emergency."
Number of People On Board (POB): State the number of people on board. "We have [Number] people on board."
Type of Assistance Needed: Specify the type of help you require. "We require immediate assistance," "We require medical evacuation," "We require a tow."
"Over": End your transmission with "Over" and release the transmit button to listen for a response.
Example Mayday Call: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, Sailing Vessel Serenity, Sailing Vessel Serenity, Sailing Vessel Serenity. Position is 34 degrees 25 minutes North, 118 degrees 30 minutes West, approximately 10 miles south of Catalina Island. We are taking on water and sinking. Four people on board. Requesting immediate assistance. Over."

Remain on Channel 16 (or 22A as instructed) and listen for a response. Be prepared to provide further information as requested by the Coast Guard or other responding vessels.

Pan Pan (Pronounced "Pahn Pahn"): Urgent Situations, Not Immediate Danger – Priority Assistance Needed

"Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan" (from the French "panne," meaning breakdown) is the urgency signal used for situations that are urgent but do not pose an immediate threat to life or the vessel. It indicates a situation where priority assistance is needed, but there is no imminent danger of loss of life or sinking.

Examples of Pan Pan situations: Engine failure in a busy shipping channel, a serious but stable medical situation, a non-life-threatening navigational hazard.

The Pan Pan call procedure is similar to Mayday:

Channel Selection: Use Channel 16 initially, or you can use another appropriate channel if you know who you are trying to reach (e.g., a specific marina).
Transmit: Press the transmit button and clearly and slowly say: "Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan".
Identify Vessel, Location, Nature of Urgency, Assistance Needed, POB (as with Mayday).
Example Pan Pan Call: "Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Motor Vessel Wanderer, Motor Vessel Wanderer, Motor Vessel Wanderer. Position is approximately one mile east of the harbor entrance buoy at Anytown. We have suffered complete engine failure and are drifting towards rocks. Requesting tow assistance to harbor. Two people on board. Over."

Listen for a response on the channel you transmitted on. Be prepared to switch channels if instructed.

Question: How long should I wait before repeating my MAYDAY call?

Repeat the full MAYDAY call after four minutes. Do this correctly and the distress call is repeated to increase the chances of receiving assistance. Just be careful: do not confuse the four-minute repeat interval with the fifteen-second wait for DSC.

The words “THIS IS”, spoken once.
Name of the vessel in distress (spoken three times) and call sign or boat registration number, spoken once. *TIP: have this information written and nearby the VHF for anyone onboard calling a mayday. Seconds count in an emergency!

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

[Excerpt 3 — Essential_Guide_VHF.txt / essential_guide_vhf]
"Mayday, Mayday, Mayday" is the internationally recognized distress call, used only when a vessel is facing imminent and grave danger – a situation where there is an immediate threat to life or the vessel is in danger of sinking or being destroyed.

Using Mayday is reserved for true emergencies. Examples include: sinking, fire, serious medical emergency, man overboard in dangerous conditions.

The Mayday call procedure is specific and should be followed precisely:

Channel Selection: Immediately switch your marine VHF radio to Channel 16 (or Channel 22A if Channel 16 is congested, but Channel 16 is primary).
Transmit: Press the transmit button and clearly and slowly say: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday".
Identify Vessel: State: "This is [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel]". Repeat your boat name three times.
Location: Clearly state your position. Use GPS coordinates if possible, or describe your location relative to landmarks. "My position is [Latitude and Longitude] " or "We are [Number] miles [Direction] of [Landmark]."
Nature of Emergency: Briefly and clearly describe the nature of your emergency. "We are sinking," "We are on fire," "We have a serious medical emergency."
Number of People On Board (POB): State the number of people on board. "We have [Number] people on board."
Type of Assistance Needed: Specify the type of help you require. "We require immediate assistance," "We require medical evacuation," "We require a tow."
"Over": End your transmission with "Over" and release the transmit button to listen for a response.
Example Mayday Call: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, Sailing Vessel Serenity, Sailing Vessel Serenity, Sailing Vessel Serenity. Position is 34 degrees 25 minutes North, 118 degrees 30 minutes West, approximately 10 miles south of Catalina Island. We are taking on water and sinking. Four people on board. Requesting immediate assistance. Over."

Remain on Channel 16 (or 22A as instructed) and listen for a response. Be prepared to provide further information as requested by the Coast Guard or other responding vessels.

Pan Pan (Pronounced "Pahn Pahn"): Urgent Situations, Not Immediate Danger – Priority Assistance Needed

"Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan" (from the French "panne," meaning breakdown) is the urgency signal used for situations that are urgent but do not pose an immediate threat to life or the vessel. It indicates a situation where priority assistance is needed, but there is no imminent danger of loss of life or sinking.

Examples of Pan Pan situations: Engine failure in a busy shipping channel, a serious but stable medical situation, a non-life-threatening navigational hazard.

The Pan Pan call procedure is similar to Mayday:

Channel Selection: Use Channel 16 initially, or you can use another appropriate channel if you know who you are trying to reach (e.g., a specific marina).
Transmit: Press the transmit button and clearly and slowly say: "Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan".
Identify Vessel, Location, Nature of Urgency, Assistance Needed, POB (as with Mayday).
Example Pan Pan Call: "Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Motor Vessel Wanderer, Motor Vessel Wanderer, Motor Vessel Wanderer. Position is approximately one mile east of the harbor entrance buoy at Anytown. We have suffered complete engine failure and are drifting towards rocks. Requesting tow assistance to harbor. Two people on board. Over."

Listen for a response on the channel you transmitted on. Be prepared to switch channels if instructed.

Question: How do I escalate from a PAN PAN to a MAYDAY?

First, acknowledge MRCC requests and follow a fixed schedule for updates; Then, use the correct format for each level of distress call; Next, escalate the distress signal appropriately as conditions worsen. Do this correctly and consistent updates keep the MRCC informed and prepared. Just be careful: sending an unwarranted MAYDAY can divert resources from genuine emergencies.

[Excerpt 1 — Securite_Mayday_Repeat_And_Escalation_Sequences.txt / Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences]
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIFE ZERO DECIMAL WUN TOO NORTH ZERO ZERO WUN DECIMAL FOWER FIFE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN WUN FIFE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

[Excerpt 2 — Routine_Prowords_Urgency_Call_Examples.txt / Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations]
Once a person overboard has been recovered unharmed, a PAN PAN cancellation or "all clear" broadcast should follow so other stations do not continue diverting resources. Example: "ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEANEX, OCEANEX, OCEANEX, PAN PAN CANCEL, PERSON OVERBOARD RECOVERED SAFELY, NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OUT."

[Excerpt 3 — Routine_Prowords_Urgency_Call_Examples.txt / Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations]
If unsure whether a situation is serious enough for a formal PAN PAN, call the coastguard first on their working channel and ask for advice rather than escalating immediately. Example: "SOLENT COASTGUARD, THIS IS PELAGIC, ROUTINE, REQUEST ADVICE, OVER." After describing the situation factually, the coastguard will advise whether to declare a formal urgency call, continue monitoring, or stand down. This avoids both over-reacting and under-reacting to a developing situation.

Question: When should I use a PAN PAN MEDICO call?
Only escalate to MAYDAY if there is grave and imminent danger to life, provided that do not use MAYDAY for routine assistance or non-immediate danger situations.

Distress calls/messages have absolute priority over all other communications. When heard, all other transmissions should cease and a listening watch should be kept. Any distress call/message should be recorded in the ship’s log and passed to the master. On receipt of a distress message, if in the vicinity, immediately acknowledge receipt. If not in the vicinity, allow a short interval of time to elapse before acknowledging receipt of the message in order to permit ships nearer to the distress to do so.

[Excerpt 2 — DSC_Menu_And_EPIRB_SART_Operation.txt / Dsc Radio Menu Operation And Epirb/Sart Handling]
A DSC distress alert is sent by lifting (or flipping open) the dedicated DISTRESS button cover and pressing and holding the DISTRESS button for approximately five seconds, until the radio confirms the alert has been sent (usually a beep and a change of display). If time and safety allow, the operator should also select the nature of distress (fire, flooding, collision, and so on) from the short menu presented before the five-second hold completes; if there is no time, an undesignated distress alert with position and time is still sent and can be corrected later. After sending the DSC distress alert, the operator should immediately follow up with a voice MAYDAY call on Channel 16.

[Excerpt 3 — MarinePublicVHF.txt / Emergency Distress Procedures]
❕ Important: Distress button remains non-functional until proper MMSI programming completion during initial system setup.

Cancel the declared situation. Do this correctly and other stations are informed that assistance is no longer required.

[Excerpt 1 — marine_vhf_radio_sample_pages.pdf / 8. Marine communications equipment]
SOLAS vessels are fitted with GMDSS equipment according to the sea areas in which they operate. Smaller vessels (merchant ships, fishing boats, superyachts, etc) comply with the carriage requirements of regional or national regulations. Also, when the safety of life is the key factor, pleasure boats are fitted with simplified GMDSS equipment. Marine VHF radios with DSC controllers are now the equipment of choice for communi- cations at sea. Marine MF/HF SSB radios also have integrated DSC with dedicated watch receivers for long-range communications and for providing access to a wealth of resources: weather data, email contact with friends and family, etc. Satellite EPIRB beacons, now with integrated GPS, provide a secondary means of distress alerting, which removes the “search” from search-and-rescue operations. The Navtex receiver receives and displays as plain text maritime safety information such as navigational and gale warnings and search-and-rescue information. The Automated Identification System (AIS) is an onboard system to transmit the name, characteristics, course and speed of commercial vessels on the high seas on VHF radio frequencies, mainly to avoid collisions between vessels when transiting areas of high vessel traffic. Radar SART facilitates the location of lifeboats or rescue rafts, as do the new AIS–SART systems. Satellite communications offer simple and reliable alternatives but with a higher oper- ating cost. Among them are Inmarsat C stations for distress and slow data transmis- sions, as well as Iridium satellite phones with global coverage.

[Excerpt 2 — marine_vhf_radio_sample_pages.pdf / 7. The Global Maritime Distress and Safety System]
The Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) is an international system using advanced communications technology designed to enhance ship-to-shore communications and provide automated distress alerting. Compliance is mandatory for SOLAS vessels (large cargo and passenger ships) on international voyages or in open seas. For smaller fishing boats and commercial vessels, the availability of GMDSS equipment is required by the national legislation of maritime countries (with reduced carriage requirements). At present, GMDSS is voluntary for small craft and pleasure boats, but a growing number of vessels are fitted with GMDSS radiocommunications equipment and can take advantage of the benefits of this distress and safety system. The principle of GMDSS is that search-and-rescue authorities ashore, as well as shipping in the immediate vicinity of a ship in distress, will be rapidly alerted to a distress incident so that they can assist in a coordinated Search and Rescue (SAR) operation with the minimum of delay. The system also provides for the promulgation of Maritime Safety Information (MSI), for example navigational and meteorological warnings and forecasts and other urgent safety information to ships. GMDSS ensures in the whole world the totality of the radiocommunications necessary for safeguarding human life at sea. You must therefore carefully consider the options that are available to you, thinking about your own needs for training and equipment in order to understand and use GMDSS.

The Ship Portable Radio licence allows a named licensee to have one VHF portable maritime radio for use on different vessels, using a “T number” call sign.  (The radio must have an integral antenna and power supply).  Other radio equipment such as one EPIRB/PLB can also be included; further details are available at: http://www.ofcom.org.uk/radiocomms/ifi/licensing/classes/maritime /information/of168a.pdf The Ship Portable Radio Licence is intended for use in UK territorial waters only. Obtaining a Ship radio or Ship Portable Radio licence – online Since December 2006, using the Ofcom website, boat owners have been able to apply online free of charge for a new licence or to amend the details of an existing one.  Paper based applications are subject to a one off fee of £20. Although there is no end date on the licence, licensees must validate their licence at least once every ten years.  There is no charge for validating your licence, and it can be done either online or by using a paper based application form. There is no charge for amending (or validating licences), whether done on-line or by post. If a licensee sells their vessel it is important for them to surrender their licence.  This can be done online or by using a paper based form. Should they purchase a vessel they should apply for a new licence indicating the details of the vessel’s call sign and Maritime Mobile Service Identity where applicable, as these must remain with the vessel. It is still a legal requirement for vessel owners that have radio equipment with access to international channels on board their vessel, to have an up-to-date radio licence.  They must keep these on board where practicable and in any case must be kept on board www.rya.org.uk

[Excerpt 1 — 5CVHF.txt / 5cvhf]
The marine industry is unique. Aviation relies on oversight with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) directing traffic via voice radio communication to avoid aircraft incidents. Railroads use radio communication, along with visual signals, but again with oversight by the operators of the rail line. With maritime, as far as collision avoidance and Rules of the Road compliance are concerned, vessels rely on mutual agreement primarily using radio communication. Sound signals are specified in the Rules of the Road but, in reality, are only a backup. Even in Vessel Traffic System (VTS)-controlled areas, the arrangements for meeting and passing have to be agreed upon between the individual vessels, again utilizing VHF radio communication.

The U.S. Federal Communication Commission (FCC) is responsible for publishing and enforcing the regulations for all radio communication. This includes U.S.-flagged vessels and foreign vessels when navigating in our regulated areas. The mariner should periodically review these regulations which are available on the Internet and are published in various FCC documents. Most of these regulations deal with types of equipment, types of operator’s licenses and assigned frequencies, but very little is devoted to procedures and nothing is discussed about proper radio etiquette. For the most part, VHF radio procedures and etiquette have been accepted practices, passed down from one generation of mariners to the next.

If you consider what is involved, this is really amazing. The professional pilots, masters, mates and everyone who is part of this industry can be very proud of maintaining and using a system that needs little oversight and hasn’t changed significantly since VHF radio communication took over from whistle signals as the primary means of Rules of the Road compliance. Through the years there have been many advances with all maritime communication, especially with the incorporation of Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) on commercial vessels, but the basic voice VHF bridge-to-bridge communication system has remained unchanged. Every professional mariner with whom I have discussed this subject has agreed that, no matter what, the party-line vessel-to-vessel communication system, generally using VHF Channel 13, has to be preserved. Every master or pilot wants to hear a voice spoken by the person conning the other vessel, either proposing or acknowledging an agreed upon action.

What do we need to do to keep this system efficient and effective? Some general guidelines, mostly common sense, have evolved over the years. Most apply to usage of VHF Channel 13 and Rules of the Road compliance, but they are appropriate for all VHF radio communications.

Good radio communication can be expressed using four “C” words that are easy to remember: CLEAR, COMPLETE, CONCISE, and CORRECT. There is a fifth “C” word, that is in a category all its own because of its often overlooked importance, “COURTEOUS.”

CLEAR: When you first learned to talk, you learned that there is an inside voice and an outside voice. As the years went along, you learned that there is a conversational voice, a stern voice and a happy voice. Then you learned a public speaking voice and even a telephone voice. There is also a proper “Radio Voice.” It is lower and slower with very clear pronunciation, especially with the consonants. Mumbling, after it gets transmitted and received through all the electronics, can be unintelligible. Try speaking various ways into the recorder on your iPhone and chose the tone and pronunciation that is the clearest and easiest to understand.

COMPLETE: Federal regulations CFR Title 47, Subpart C, 80.102 requires that every ship and shore station identify themselves by the appropriate call sign at the beginning and end of every transmission. There is provision that the vessel’s, or authorized shore station’s name can be substituted for the call sign, but only on VHF Channel 13.  The accepted interpretation of this CFR is that every transmission should have the name of the vessel or shore station included at least once in every transmission. The most common protocol is to start the transmission with the vessel’s name that you are calling to get their attention, followed by your identity.  Example: “Tug Captain Henry T. O’Brian, this is the tanker Sinclair Ohio.”

Some vessels’ names are long or hard to pronounce, but, after an initial contact, can be abbreviated to cut down on the air time as long as the individual identity is preserved, i.e., Captain Henry T. O’Brian can become “Henry T.” for a repeated transmission (unless the Captain Henry T. Littlefield is also in the area).

Every transmission should include at least one complete sentence. With radio transmissions, especially when using VHF Channel 13, brevity is good, but you still must express a complete thought, i.e. “Henry T. – One” is too brief. “Captain Henry T. acknowledges one whistle meeting the vessel’s name” is better.

Federal regulations CFR Title 47, Subpart C, 80.89 states, in part, that every VHF transmission is only allowed between two ship stations or a ship station and a shore station with the exemption of general safety calls, urgent calls, or distress calls. General safety calls are prefaced by the French word “sécurité,” which almost everyone incorrectly pronounces as “security,” repeated three times. Urgent calls, which are rarely used, are prefaced by the word group “pan-pan,” commonly pronounced “pon-pon” from the French word “panne,” repeated three times. Distress calls are prefaced by the word “mayday,” repeated three times. Radio checks are allowed, but strongly discouraged on VHF Channel 13, and only by authorized personnel on VHF Channel 16. Radio traffic between vessels and aircraft are allowed in very limited situations.

General safety calls on VHF Channel 13 are routinely used when leaving a berth or anchorage, approaching a blind turn, or about to enter or block a main navigational channel. Also, some ports have established suggested locations where vessels broadcast general safety calls when passing, i.e., inbound at Norton Point in New York Harbor, eastbound in the C&D canal at Biddle Point. Generally these are just common sense, but sometimes they are published in the appropriate Coast Pilot or other local knowledge publications. General safety calls are very important and should be used, but not overused. All vessels listen when they hear “sécurité, sécurité, sécurité,” or “security, security, security.”

CONCISE: If you want to discuss something at length, wait until you are face to face, call on a cell phone or use another channel. VHF Channel 13 communication is for short and focused communication. An example of a communication that is too long and complex is: “This is the tug Bridgett T. answering the outbound ship. I intend to meet you on one whistle on the straightaway. To do that, I am going to slow down to 600 rpm at buoy 7 and then slow down to clutch at buoy 8. At buoy 8, I’ll proceed over to the red side of the channel to meet you on one whistle, over.” The pertinent information can be transmitted more concisely as: “This is the tug Bridgett T. I will meet the outbound ship on one whistle. I’ll slow down so that we will meet on the straightaway.” The shorter the better as long as you get your basic point across without leaving something important out or sounding too abrupt.

CORRECT: It used to be the accepted practice to fib, just a little. Position reports were ahead of where you really were and speeds were on the high side using optimistic calculations. Now with GPS, chart plotters and particularly AIS, this just isn’t necessary. Other vessels are relying on the information you are giving them, especially with regards to your intentions, so keep it as accurate as possible.

COURTESY: When I start a discussion with other professionals about this subject, this aspect of communication always prompts some interesting conversations. There is a lot that can be said about this subject, but the following simple guideline is the most important.

Every VHF Channel 13 radio communication has one very simple objective: a positive outcome. No matter if the person that you are communicating with happens to be an archrival, your best friend or a complete stranger, it still comes down to the fact that what you discuss and decide has to work out right. The very best way to do this is with courteous radio communication. Sarcasm, cynicism, disdain, condescension or contempt are almost always counterproductive. If you want to argue with someone, join a blog, or call them on a cell phone. Radio communication, especially on VHF Channel 13, is a business-only medium.

Before pushing the Push to Talk button to start communication, take a moment to think through what you are going to say. Does it have a disrespectful tone to it? Could it be taken the wrong way? If you are courteous during your transmission you will prompt a courteous reply and, most important, a good conclusion.

Over the past several years, recreational and other non-required vessels have been encouraged to monitor and answer when called on VHF Channel 13 when navigating in or close to main shipping channels. This has been working out very well and should be encouraged as it has avoided some close-call situations, especially at night and during reduced visibility. This means that there are many more vessels monitoring VHF Channel 13, making good radio etiquette all the more important.

Looking to the future, vessels that will be navigating along our coast and into our ports will be larger with the expansion of the Panama Canal. Navigation into and out of ports will be more complex with wind turbine farms and other structures being placed along our coast and in our bays. Navigational systems will certainly become more sophisticated with more powerful computer systems and advanced electronic aids to navigation. There certainly will be precautionary areas, traffic separation schemes and two-way routes established to assist mariners as they navigate in and out of our ports and along our coast. The navigational systems that professional mariners rely on today weren’t even imagined just a few decades ago. Staying ahead of these changes has and will be a challenge for all mariners. What will remain, however, is that VHF radio communication will be the primary means of Rules of the Road compliance and marine safety and traffic information.

Discuss good radio procedures and etiquette with other professionals in your groups. Go through this subject with your trainees and be a good example by practicing what you preach. It may be difficult, but if someone is doing something wrong, talk to them about it (but not on VHF Channel 13). If you have an idea of how to make communications better, discuss your ideas with your co-workers or put it out for discussion with the appropriate Harbor Safety Committees. Good radio etiquette has been and will be very important in order to continue and improve this unique and very effective system into the future.

[Excerpt 2 — SailingBlogVHF.txt / Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio]
My brothers and I grew up in a sailing family. We had a 27-foot Catalina that we’d take out on the weekends any time the weather was nice and even when the weather wasn’t nice, we’d often still find ourselves on the boat, helping to scrub the decks and maintain the gear. On those days, we’d inevitably get bored, at which point the VHF radio would become a serious temptation. One day, when our dad was occupied somewhere on the bow, I grabbed the radio and said something silly. Before I could crack another joke, my dad was over top of me, grabbing the receiver out of my hand. I never knew he could move that fast! I learned the importance of VHF radio etiquette that day, and it’s a lesson I’ve never forgotten.

Your VHF radio is your best way to communicate with other boats on the water, with marinas, and with the coast guard, if necessary. VHF stands for “Very High Frequency.” It’s the standard form of communication on the water, is more reliable than cell phones, and it’s always being monitored. Learning to use it, however, is a little like learning a new language. You can’t just hop on and start talking.

Below are the basics, and you can learn VHF usage in-depth in NauticEd’s Bareboat Charter Clinic.

Always be listening
Using a VHF marine radioYour VHF radio is a safety tool. Even if you don’t need to communicate with anyone, you should be listening for important weather updates and other announcements on channel 16. This is especially true if you’re boating in high-traffic areas or locations where weather can change quickly. You don’t have to have it blaring beside you and not let anyone else on the boat speak (not exactly our idea of a good sail), but you’ll want to have it on while you’re in transit.

And note there are certain regulations that require you to keep a “Radio Watch” at all times. The rules state that in general, any vessel equipped with a VHF marine radiotelephone must maintain a watch on channel 16 (156.8MHz) whenever the radiotelephone is not being used to communicate.

Brush up on your VHF lingo
VHF communication has its own set of terms that have developed over the last century. These were originally brief, clear words and ideas that could be easily transmitted over telegraph. As vocal communication developed, these terms continued to develop and were used to keep communications brief and to avoid confusion and miscommunication. These terms are often called “procedure words,” or “prowords.” You can find exhaustive lists online, but here are a few basic ones that are good to know.

[Excerpt 3 — marine_vhf_radio_sample_pages.pdf / 66 Marine VHF Radio Handbook Chapter 4]
Example: on board Neptune during an Atlantic crossing, you meet an oil tanker under flag of Malta. You want to contact it, but you cannot read the tanker’s name. Send your national flag and contact the tanker by VHF on channel 16, like this: Northwest bound tanker with red funnel. This is Neptune, Neptune, the British yacht on your port side. Do you read me? Over. As the tanker keeps aural watch on channel 16, normally you would hear its answer: Station calling on channel 16. This is oil tanker Marbella. Please say again your name and call sign. Over. You answer on channel 16: Marbella, this is Neptune, call sign Foxtrot Lima Six Two Zero Five. Good afternoon. Could you please give me the last weather forecast for this area? Over. Still on channel 16, Marbella proposes to switch to channel 08: Neptune, this is Marbella. Good afternoon. Advise you change to VHF channel zero eight. Over. Neptune confirms the change of channel on channel 16, before changing channel: Marbella, this is Neptune, changing to VHF channel zero eight. Over. Marbella continues on channel 08: Neptune, this is Marbella. The weather forecast for the area at 1200 hours UTC is …. Do you need anything else? What is your destination? Over. Neptune says goodbye on channel 08: Marbella, this is Neptune. Thank you very much, nothing else. My destination is Gibraltar. We expect to … Over. The deck officer of Marbella on channel 08: Neptune, this is Marbella. Have a good trip. Fair winds. Out.

**Source:** International Maritime Organization (IMO), International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, Chapter IV
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/About/Conventions/Pages/International-Convention-for-the-Safety-of-Life-at-Sea-(SOLAS),-1974.aspx

SOLAS is the core international treaty governing ship safety, and Chapter IV of its Annex deals specifically with radiocommunications. Its purpose is to guarantee that ships covered by the Convention are equipped so they can reliably send and receive distress and safety information, coordinate with each other and with shore authorities in emergencies, and call on organized search-and-rescue services when needed. The chapter also ensures that radio installations across different vessels and shore stations are technically compatible with one another, that they remain functional even after a single equipment failure (i.e., there is built-in redundancy), and that they are properly maintained throughout a ship's operational life.

Chapter IV applies to all passenger ships on international voyages and to cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage or more on international voyages. It underpins the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), the internationally standardized system of satellite and terrestrial communication procedures used for maritime distress alerting.

The chapter has been substantially revised over time to keep pace with changing technology. A major modernization came into force on 1 January 2024 (via IMO Resolution MSC.496(105)), which updated the GMDSS to reflect the shift away from older systems. Under the revised chapter, ships operating in certain sea areas (A3/A4) are no longer required to carry high-frequency narrow-band direct-printing telegraphy (HF NBDP) equipment for transmitting and receiving distress and safety messages, and NAVTEX/EGC/HF NBDP receivers are no longer automatically mandatory — although owners may retain such equipment voluntarily for receiving maritime safety information. The amendments also broadened recognition of satellite service providers beyond Inmarsat to include other "Recognized Mobile Satellite Service" providers, such as Iridium, where a flag state accepts them.

In UK law, SOLAS Chapter IV's requirements are given direct legal effect through the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 (see Section 2 below), and MCA Marine Guidance Note 641 (M) explains how UK-flagged ships and operators should apply it in practice.

.A Selcall number is a code which when programmed into a radio receiver will ensure that the receiver will respond only to calls addressed to it. .This system is becoming obsolete and Ofcom does not envisage licensing any new Selcall numbers unless specifically requested.

[Excerpt 2 — Talk_Like_Old_Salt.txt / talk_like_old_salt]
When you’re transmitting numbers, you should always say them in a digital format. For instance, instead of saying “twenty-two”, you should say “two-two”. This ensures that the numbers are clearly transmitted and there’s no confusion. Also, when saying the number nine, it’s common to use the term “niner” since nine is often confused for five.

[Excerpt 3 — NATO_Phonetic_Alphabet.txt / Nato Phonetic Alphabet]
Numbers are also given their own standardized pronunciation on VHF radio to avoid confusion, particularly between numbers that sound alike when spoken quickly. Zero is pronounced ZERO. One is pronounced WUN. Two is pronounced TOO. Three is pronounced TREE. Four is pronounced FOWER. Five is pronounced FIFE. Six is pronounced SIX. Seven is pronounced SEVEN. Eight is pronounced AIT. Nine is pronounced NINER. Each digit of a multi-digit number, such as a call sign or a position, is read out individually rather than as a whole number, for example the number 79 is transmitted as SEVEN NINER, not as seventy-nine.

Why the Phonetic Alphabet Matters

Using the correct phonetic alphabet is not optional politeness, it is a regulatory requirement under the ITU Radio Regulations because misheard letters in a vessel name, call sign, or position can delay a search and rescue response or cause a message to be logged incorrectly by a coast station or Vessel Traffic Service. Before transmitting a spelled-out word, the operator should say "I SPELL" so the listening station knows individual letters are about to follow rather than a normal word, and should read the word back once at normal pace afterward so the listener can confirm they understood correctly.

Because a Selcall number ensures a radio receiver responds only to specific calls, and because ofcom does not plan to license new Selcall numbers unless there is a specific request.

An MMSI number is required before the equipment can be commissioned. .If an MMSI has already been issued for use with DSC equipment and subsequentlyasatellite earth station terminal is installed, if a new MMSI is required, the DSC equipment may need to be re-programmed. What is Channel 16 on the marine VHF radio?
Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency for marine VHF radios, operating at 156.800 MHz. It serves as the universal emergency channel monitored continuously by the Coast Guard and is used for MAYDAY calls and initial hailing before switching to working channels.

What is usually on channel 16?
Channel 16 typically carries distress calls, emergency communications, initial hailing between vessels, Coast Guard safety broadcasts, and navigation warnings. It is monitored by rescue authorities 24/7 but should never be used for routine conversation.

How to use VHF channel 16?
Use Channel 16 only for emergencies or brief hailing. To hail another station, call their name twice, identify yourself, and say over. After contact, immediately switch to a working channel like 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78A for actual conversation. For emergencies, make MAYDAY calls on Channel 16 and remain there for rescue coordination.

How to use a VHF marine radio for beginners?
First, select the appropriate channel. Second, adjust squelch until static disappears. Third, press and hold the PTT button. Fourth, speak normally holding the mic 2 inches from your mouth. Fifth, release PTT to listen. Practice on Channel 9 for radio checks before using Channel 16.

Is Channel 16 for emergency?
Yes, Channel 16 is the primary emergency channel for marine VHF radios. It is used for MAYDAY distress calls when life is in danger. The Coast Guard monitors Channel 16 continuously and responds immediately to emergency calls. However, Channel 16 is also used for non-emergency hailing, so keep transmissions brief and switch to working channels promptly.

When to use Channel 16?
Use Channel 16 for three situations only: life-threatening emergencies requiring MAYDAY calls, initial hailing of other vessels or shore stations before switching channels, and responding to hails from others. Never use Channel 16 for routine conversation, weather checks, or radio testing. Monitor Channel 16 continuously while underway to hear emergency calls.

Conclusion
Learning how to use a marine VHF radio and Channel 16 is an investment in your safety and confidence on the water. Unlike cell phones that fail when you need them most, a properly operated VHF radio connects you to rescue services, other boaters, and essential information anywhere your boat can reach. The skills covered in this guide, from basic operation to emergency procedures, become automatic with practice.

Start by mastering the five basic steps: selecting the right channel, adjusting squelch, pushing PTT, speaking normally, and releasing to listen. Keep Channel 16 monitored while underway for safety broadcasts and emergency awareness. Practice hailing on working channels before you need to make emergency calls. Understanding the difference between MAYDAY, Pan-Pan, and Securite ensures you get the right level of response when situations arise.

If you are new to radio operation, work through the practice exercises in this guide. Build your confidence with radio checks and routine marina hailing. Before long, you will communicate like an experienced captain. Your VHF radio is your most reliable connection to safety on the water. Learn to use it properly in 2026, and every trip becomes safer and more enjoyable.

There are three different levels of safety or distress calls, which boaters can use to let other boats in the area know of potential or real danger. Distress calls are initiated on Channel 16 (and a reason you always monitor it).  If you hear or receive a distress call and cannot assist, immediately cease all transmission on Channel 16! Any vessel with knowledge of distress traffic who cannot assist is forbidden from transmitting on a distress channel (until you receive the “all clear”).

MAYDAY: This is an urgent and immediate distress call, made when a boat is in danger of sinking or there is a fire, man overboard, or medical emergency on board. Vessels that are close enough to help are required to do so. You should only make a mayday call if you are in serious or immediate danger. If you have a VHF marine radio, tune it to channel 16. Unless you know you are outside VHF range of shore and ships, call on channel 16 first.
A Mayday distress signal is first spoken three times, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY”.
The words “THIS IS”, spoken once.
Name of the vessel in distress (spoken three times) and call sign or boat registration number, spoken once. *TIP: have this information written and nearby the VHF for anyone onboard calling a mayday. Seconds count in an emergency!
Repeat “MAYDAY” and name of vessel, spoken once.
Give position of the vessel by latitude or longitude or by bearing (true or magnetic, state which) and distance to a well-known landmark such as a navigational aid or small island, or in any terms which will assist a responding station in locating the vessel in distress. Include any information on vessel movement such as course, speed and destination.
Nature of distress (sinking, fire etc.).
Kind of assistance desired.
The number of persons onboard.
Any other information which might facilitate rescue, such as length or tonnage of the vessel, number of persons needing medical attention, color hull, cabin, masks, etc.
The word “OVER”

[Excerpt 2 — BoatUS.txt / boatus]
Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

[Excerpt 2 — VHFIMOSummaries.txt / Further Reading — Summaries]
**Source:** Office of Communications (Ofcom)
**Link:** https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/ships-radio

This is Ofcom's guidance on the licensing regime for radio equipment carried on ships, covering medium frequency (MF), VHF, high frequency (HF), and ultra-high frequency (UHF) radio equipment, as well as satellite communications, radar, Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and Search and Rescue Transponders (SARTs). The stated purposes of licensing are twofold: to prevent radio equipment from causing undue interference to other users of the spectrum, and to ensure equipment is operated only by competent, appropriately trained individuals.

Historically a UK "Ship Radio Licence" required annual renewal and a fee, but following a 2005 Ofcom consultation and policy change, ships' radio licences became "lifetime" licences from 1 October 2006 — free of charge, issued electronically, with no fixed expiry date, remaining valid as long as the registered details stay accurate (though licensees must periodically reconfirm their details). A licence is personal to the licensee and does not automatically transfer if a vessel is sold. Separately from the equipment licence, the individual operating the radio needs an operator's qualification — for VHF-only use this is the Short Range Certificate (SRC), obtained via a one-day training course covering radio procedure, etiquette, and use of Digital Selective Calling (DSC); a Long Range Certificate (LRC) is needed for other, longer-range communications equipment.

Operating marine radio equipment without both the required ship licence and a valid operator's certificate is a criminal offence. Ofcom's enforcement team can issue on-the-spot fines, and the maximum penalty on conviction is a £5,000 fine and/or up to six months' imprisonment, with the possibility of forfeiture of any radio apparatus used unlawfully. This is the direct legal underpinning of the PLA bulletin's warning that improper VHF use may lead to penalties enforced by Ofcom.

This is Ofcom's guidance on the licensing regime for radio equipment carried on ships, covering medium frequency (MF), VHF, high frequency (HF), and ultra-high frequency (UHF) radio equipment, as well as satellite communications, radar, Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and Search and Rescue Transponders (SARTs). The stated purposes of licensing are twofold: to prevent radio equipment from causing undue interference to other users of the spectrum, and to ensure equipment is operated only by competent, appropriately trained individuals.

[Excerpt 3 — VHFIMOSummaries.txt / Further Reading — Summaries]
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/radio-equipment-regulations-2017

These Regulations set out the technical and safety requirements that radio equipment (including marine VHF sets) must meet before they can legally be placed on the UK market or put into service. They were originally made to implement the EU's Radio Equipment Directive (2014/53/EU) into UK law and have since been adapted for the UK's post-Brexit UKCA (UK Conformity Assessed) marking regime, distinct from the EU's CE marking.

The Regulations' "essential requirements" (broadly in regulation/Article 3) require that radio equipment be constructed so that it protects the health and safety of users and other people (including domestic animals) and property; that it achieves an adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility, meaning it neither causes excessive interference to other equipment nor is itself unduly affected by interference; and that it makes effective use of the radio spectrum so as to avoid causing harmful interference to other radio users — a point directly relevant to why "unnecessary transmission" and "non-standard phrases" on VHF are discouraged, since spectrum efficiency is a legal design and use consideration, not just an etiquette one.

The Regulations place obligations on the various "economic operators" in the supply chain — manufacturers, importers, and distributors — including duties to prepare technical documentation, ensure conformity assessment procedures are followed, cooperate with enforcement authorities, and withdraw non-conforming equipment from the market if concerns are identified. Ofcom has powers to evaluate and act against radio equipment that presents a risk. The Regulations exclude certain categories of equipment from their scope, including some radio amateur and marine equipment governed by separate regimes, and they allow for different requirements in Northern Ireland reflecting its distinct post-Brexit trading arrangements.
